question: As of April 19, 2023, what evidence established whether OPEC and its partner countries had begun implementing the additional crude-oil production cuts announced on April 3?

answer_points.text: EIA reported an April 3 announcement of plans to cut crude-oil production by 1.2 million b/d through end-2023; this passage establishes plans, not actual implementation.

EIA lowered its OPEC crude-production forecast for 2Q23–4Q23 by around 0.5 million b/d because it had already allowed for some reductions; neither that forecast revision nor the reported March undershoot establishes execution of the additional April 3 cuts.

quotes.text: On April 3, OPEC and partner countries (OPEC+) announced plans to cut crude oil production by 1.2 million barrels per day (b/d) through the end of 2023.
In March, OPEC produced less than its previous targets, and in our March STEO, we had assumed that OPEC production would fall further below the prior production targets in the coming month.

Because we had already accounted for some of the reduction in crude oil output from OPEC countries subject to the cuts, we have reduced our forecast for OPEC’s crude oil production from the second quarter of 2023 (2Q23) through 4Q23 by around 0.5 million b/d.

reasons: The eligible pool documents the announcement and forecast response but gives no post-announcement production observations establishing whether implementation had begun by April 19. Later sources are ineligible.

question: In EIA’s June 2025 outlook for the Gulf of America, how were fields expected to start production in 2025–2026 divided between subsea tiebacks and new floating production units, and what crude-oil contribution was forecast for each year?

answer_points.text: Of 13 fields expected to start production in 2025–2026, eight would use subsea tiebacks or underwater extensions to existing FPUs, and five would use four new FPUs; Salamanca would serve two fields.
EIA forecast additional crude-oil production from all the new fields of 85,000 b/d in 2025 and 308,000 b/d in 2026.

quotes.text: We expect operators to start crude oil and natural gas production at 13 fields in the GOA during 2025 and 2026, without which GOA production would decline. Eight fields will be developed using subsea tiebacks or underwater extensions to existing Floating Production Units (FPUs) at the surface. Five fields will produce from four new FPUs, with one of the new FPUs (Salamanca FPU) targeting production from two fields.
We expect the additional crude oil production from all new fields will contribute 85,000 b/d in 2025 and 308,000 b/d in 2026.

reasons: The June 6 outlook directly provides the development split and annual forecast contributions. These are forecasts, not observed annual output or sums of peak capacities.

question: How large was Wolfcamp crude-oil production in September 2018 relative to the Permian Basin total, and which drilling and completion changes were reported to be driving productivity gains?

answer_points.text: Wolfcamp produced about 1 million b/d of crude oil in September 2018, nearly one-third of total Permian crude-oil production.

Reported productivity improvements included longer horizontal laterals, increasing from an average 2,500 feet in 2005 to more than 8,500 feet in 2018, more effective use of sand/proppant, and zipper fracturing of two or more side-by-side wells.

quotes.text: As of September 2018, the Wolfcamp accounted for about 1 million barrels of crude oil per day (b/d) and 4 billion cubic feet of natural gas per day (Bcf/d). Crude oil production in the Wolfcamp accounts for nearly one-third of total Permian crude oil production and more than one-third of Permian natural gas production.

The length of the horizontal segments, or laterals, in the Wolfcamp increased from an average of 2,500 linear feet in 2005 to more than 8,500 linear feet in 2018. Well completion efficiency has also improved, primarily by more effectively using sand, or proppant, during the hydraulic fracturing process, as well as by using zipper fracturing—the completion of two or more wells side by side.

reasons: Cutoff-eligible passages directly report September production, its regional share, and the drilling and completion changes.

question: Why did EIA repeatedly lower its 2019 global liquid-fuels demand-growth outlook through July 2019, and how did its oil-weighted GDP growth assumption change between the January and July outlooks?

answer_points.text: EIA lowered its global liquids demand-growth expectation for six consecutive months because of slower expected economic growth in major consuming countries, weaker-than-expected consumption so far in 2019, and higher crude-oil prices.

The 2019 oil-weighted GDP growth assumption fell from 2.9% in January to 2.2% in July, a 0.7-percentage-point reduction; EIA weighted country-level Oxford Economics GDP forecasts by relative oil consumption.

quotes.text: EIA has revised down its expectation for global liquids demand growth for six consecutive months. This revision reflects slower expected economic growth in many of the world’s largest oil-consuming countries, lower than expected oil consumption so far this year, and higher crude oil prices.

One of the main drivers of EIA’s global oil consumption forecast is global gross domestic product (GDP) based on country-level forecasts from Oxford Economics. EIA calculates an oil-weighted GDP by using relative magnitudes of oil consumption in each country. EIA revised the 2019 oil-weighted GDP growth rate from 2.9% in its January STEO to 2.2% in its July STEO.

reasons: The July 11 source explicitly explains the successive forecast reductions and supplies both GDP assumption endpoints.

question: According to EIA’s January 2021 estimate, what was global consumption of petroleum and other liquid fuels in 2020, how far did it fall from 2019, and how did that decline rank in the series beginning in 1980?

answer_points.text: EIA estimated global petroleum and other liquid-fuels consumption at 92.2 million b/d in 2020, down 9% from 2019—the largest decline in its series beginning in 1980.
The January 2021 outlook put the absolute annual consumption decline at 9.0 million b/d, based on preliminary data and estimates.

quotes.text: The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates that the world consumed 92.2 million barrels per day (b/d) of petroleum and other liquid fuels in 2020, a 9% decline from the previous year and the largest decline in EIA’s series that dates back to 1980.
Preliminary data and estimates indicate that global liquid fuels consumption declined by 9.0 million barrels per day (b/d) in 2020, the largest annual decline in EIA data going back to 1980.

reasons: January 2021 evidence supplies the level, percentage and absolute decline, and historical ranking. Earlier 2020 forecasts do not replace that estimate.

question: Before the March 2022 U.S. import ban, how did Russia’s share of U.S. crude-oil imports compare with its share of petroleum-product imports in 2021, and why were unfinished oils relevant to U.S. refinery feedstock supply?

answer_points.text: In 2021, Russia supplied 3% of U.S. crude-oil imports versus 20% of petroleum-product imports.

Unfinished oils comprised more than half of total U.S. petroleum imports from Russia; U.S. refineries used imported unfinished oils and fuel oil to supplement crude oil in refining, and a substantial share of the Russian unfinished oils was classified as Mazut-100.

quotes.text: In 2021, imports from Russia accounted for 8% of all U.S. petroleum imports , which includes the 3% share of crude oil imports and the 20% share of petroleum product imports.
U.S. refineries use imported unfinished oils and fuel oil as a supplement to crude oil in the refining process.
More than half of U.S. total petroleum imports from Russia in 2021 were unfinished oils. A substantial share of the unfinished oils from Russia are classified as Mazut-100 fuel oil, or M-100.

reasons: The eligible March 22 source directly gives the distinct import-share denominators and refinery-feedstock role.

question: How much did Permian crude-oil production grow in 2022, and what physical link between crude extraction and associated gas explains why oil growth also increases natural-gas supply?

answer_points.text: Permian crude-oil production increased by 12% in 2022.
Reported annual average Permian crude output rose from 4.7 million b/d in 2021 to 5.3 million b/d in 2022, an increase of about 0.6 million b/d using the rounded figures.

Associated natural gas is dissolved in crude oil under formation pressure and is released as oil is brought to the surface and pressure falls; increasing crude extraction therefore also increases associated-gas supply.

quotes.text: In 2022, production of crude oil increased in the Permian region by 12%.
That amount of output compares to an average of 5.3 million b/d in 2022 and 4.7 million b/d in 2021.

Associated natural gas refers to natural gas that is dissolved in crude oil under the pressure of a geologic formation and is then released when the pressure on the crude oil is relieved by bringing it to the surface. Increasing crude oil production in the Permian region , which spans parts of western Texas and southeastern New Mexico, is driving the growth in associated natural gas production .

reasons: Eligible evidence directly reports percentage growth and explains the physical mechanism; the approximate volume increase is calculated from rounded annual averages.

question: How did the renewable-diesel movement data introduced in EIA’s March 2024 Petroleum Supply Monthly change coverage of supply flows to the U.S. West Coast relative to the existing tanker and barge data?

answer_points.text: The March 2024 PSM added interregional renewable-diesel rail movements to existing tanker and barge coverage, enabling EIA to capture most renewable-diesel movements to the West Coast.
Existing tanker and barge data already covered renewable-diesel shipments back to 2016, including Gulf Coast-to-West Coast movements.
The new data showed rail movements growing about 50% from early 2022 to late 2023, with most rail movements destined for the West Coast.

quotes.text: In our March Petroleum Supply Monthly (PSM), we introduced data on the interregional movement of renewable diesel. These new data add to our existing tanker and barge movement coverage for renewable diesel. With the new data, we now capture most of the renewable diesel movements to the U.S. West Coast

The new movement data show that renewable diesel transport by rail is growing and that most of these rail movements are destined for the West Coast. Rail movement of renewable diesel increased about 50% from early 2022 to late 2023.
Some renewable diesel also moves by tanker or barge from the Gulf Coast to the West Coast. We report data for renewable diesel tanker and barge shipments dating back to 2016

reasons: The April 4 evidence directly identifies the additional rail coverage and its importance for West Coast flows. Undated documentation is not used to support the historical answer.

question: How did EIA’s April 2018 outlook reconcile projected growth in U.S. summer highway travel with its forecast change in motor-gasoline consumption, and what role did fleet-wide fuel efficiency play?

answer_points.text: EIA forecast summer 2018 motor-gasoline consumption at 9.6 million b/d, up only 0.2%, despite projected highway-travel growth of 1.3%, because a projected 1.2% improvement in fleet-wide fuel efficiency would partially offset travel's effect on gasoline use.

quotes.text: EIA expects U.S. motor gasoline consumption for summer 2018 to average 9.6 million b/d, up slightly (0.2%) from last summer. Summer highway travel is projected to increase by 1.3%, but its effect on motor gasoline use will be partially offset by a 1.2% increase in fleet-wide fuel efficiency.

reasons: The April 12 source explicitly reconciles projected travel and gasoline consumption through fuel-efficiency gains; all figures are forecasts.

question: What production and consumption changes underlay the projected U.S. transition to net petroleum-liquids exports in 2020 in EIA’s Annual Energy Outlook 2019 Reference case, and how was that case intended to be interpreted?

answer_points.text: The AEO2019 Reference case projected net petroleum-liquids exports in 2020 as U.S. crude oil production increased and domestic petroleum-product consumption decreased.
The Reference case was a baseline for assessing future policy or technology changes, not the most probable prediction; six other cases varied key assumptions.

quotes.text: In the Reference case, the United States becomes a net exporter of petroleum liquids in 2020 as U.S. crude oil production increases and domestic consumption of petroleum products decreases.

The Reference case is not intended to be the most probable prediction of the future, but it instead forms a baseline for estimating the effects of new policy or technology changes in the future. The other six cases show the effect of changing other key model assumptions.

reasons: Cutoff-eligible AEO2019 evidence directly states both drivers and the intended interpretation; the transition is a projection.

question: How did changes in hydrocarbon gas liquids and transportation-fuel shipments combine to determine the year-over-year change in total U.S. petroleum-product exports in the first half of 2020?

answer_points.text: First-half 2020 petroleum-product exports averaged 5.4 million b/d, up 48,000 b/d (1%) year over year because increased propane and other HGL exports more than offset falling gasoline, distillate and jet-fuel exports.
Propane exports rose 175,000 b/d (17%) to 1.22 million b/d, while distillate exports fell 72,000 b/d (6%) to 1.21 million b/d, leaving propane slightly ahead.

quotes.text: In the first half of 2020, the United States exported 5.4 million barrels per day (b/d) of petroleum products, a slight increase of 48,000 b/d (1%) from the first half of 2019. Greater exports of propane and other hydrocarbon gas liquids (HGLs) more than offset declines in U.S. exports of transportation fuels such as gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and jet fuel.

Distillate fuel oil usually accounts for the largest share of U.S. petroleum product exports, but in the first half of 2020, the United States exported slightly more propane (1.22 million b/d) than distillate fuel oil (1.21 million b/d). U.S. propane exports increased by 175,000 b/d (17%) from the same period in 2019, and U.S. distillate exports decreased by 72,000 b/d (6%).

reasons: Contemporaneous evidence directly reports the net change and offsetting product movements; later annual results are ineligible.

question: Why did EIA’s February 2021 outlook anticipate greater U.S. crude-oil imports in 2021–2022 despite a forecast domestic production recovery, and how did the projected year-end monthly production levels compare with the November 2019 peak?

answer_points.text: Domestic production and inventory draws were forecast to be insufficient for refinery needs. Net crude imports were expected to rise 1.0 million b/d in 2021 as refinery inputs increased and annual domestic production declined, then another 0.7 million b/d in 2022 as refinery-input growth exceeded production growth.
Monthly domestic crude production was forecast at 11.3 million b/d at end-2021 and 11.9 million b/d at end-2022, respectively 1.6 and 1.0 million b/d below the November 2019 peak of 12.9 million b/d.

quotes.text: EIA forecasts increases in net crude oil imports in 2021 and 2022 because domestic crude oil production and inventory draws alone will not meet the needs of U.S. refineries (Figure 3). In 2021, EIA forecasts a 1.0 million b/d increase of net crude oil imports will be required to fill a widening gap between increasing refinery inputs of crude oil and declining domestic production. Although EIA expects crude oil production will grow in 2022, growth in refinery crude oil inputs is expected to be larger, resulting in a 0.7 million b/d increase in net crude oil imports.

EIA forecasts monthly domestic crude oil production will reach 11.3 million b/d by the end of 2021 and 11.9 million b/d by the end of 2022. These values are increases from the most recent monthly average of 11.1 million b/d in November 2020 (based on data in EIA’s Petroleum Supply Monthly ) but still lower than the previous peak of 12.9 million b/d in November 2019.

reasons: February evidence explains the refinery supply gap and provides all comparison levels. Year-end monthly recovery is distinct from annual-average growth.

question: As of April 1, 2022, which U.S. monthly hydrocarbon-gas-liquids inventory periods already incorporated eligible end-user storage and which still awaited revision, and how could the expanded accounting change estimated product supplied?

answer_points.text: The March 2022 Petroleum Supply Monthly already included eligible end-user storage in January 2022 monthly HGL inventories, with subsequent months to use the expanded coverage.

Revision effects for monthly 2021 inventories back to January were available in the appendix, but revised 2021 values would enter the regular website tables only with the August 2022 Petroleum Supply Monthly and 2022 Petroleum Supply Annual.

Expanded reporting covered selected end users with at least 50,000 barrels of storage and smaller facilities able to ship by pipeline, tanker or barge; increased measured inventory builds tend to lower estimated product supplied, and vice versa.

The revisions lowered estimated February 2021 HGL consumption by nearly 80,000 b/d, while a slower October stock build raised October product supplied by 146,000 b/d, including approximately 45,000 b/d of propane.

quotes.text: Starting with yesterday’s March 2022 Petroleum Supply Monthly , monthly reported HGL inventories in January 2022 and all subsequent months will reflect stocks at all bulk terminals, including end-user storage facilities meeting the reporting requirements.

Starting in January 2021, we expanded the scope of our Monthly Bulk Terminal Report to include HGLs held by selected end users with at least 50,000 barrels of storage capacity and by smaller facilities that can ship products by pipeline, tanker, or barge.
Revisions that increase inventory builds will tend to lower our estimate of product supplied and vice versa.

In yesterday’s release, this appendix, Impact of Revisions on Major Series, 2021 , shows the effects of the survey change for total U.S. HGL inventory and, within HGLs, U.S. propane inventory for monthly values going back to January 2021. The revised data for 2021 will not appear in tables currently published on our website until the release of the August 2022 Petroleum Supply Monthly and the 2022 Petroleum Supply Annual

In February 2021, when a winter storm limited much of the petrochemical consumption in the Gulf Coast region, the revised inventories reduce product supplied by nearly 80,000 fewer barrels per day (b/d) of U.S. HGL consumption. In October 2021, when the price of propane and other HGLs rose rapidly, revised inventory data show a slower build in stocks, resulting in an additional 146,000 b/d of U.S. HGL product supplied above currently reported values, approximately 45,000 b/d of which was propane.

reasons: Evidence distinguishes expanded survey coverage, current monthly publication, and pending incorporation of 2021 revisions. Product supplied responds to stock changes, not simply stock levels.

question: As of April 20, 2023, what evidence supported attributing the stabilization of Mexico’s petroleum and liquid-fuels production since 2019 specifically to growth in private-company output?

answer_points.text: EIA reported stable petroleum and liquid-fuels production since 2019 alongside growing private production. Private production contributed more than 5% of Mexico’s total in 2022, compared with a 0.5% oil contribution in 2016.

In July 2021, EIA explicitly attributed an upward revision of its 2021 liquid-fuels production forecast from 1.8 to 1.9 million b/d to private operators exceeding expectations in ramping up Ixachi, Pokoch and Hokchi.

EIA also attributed stability to new Sureste Basin developments replacing declining older fields, citing Quesqui’s 133,000 b/d in 2022. This passage does not identify Quesqui as private production or quantify private companies’ exclusive contribution.

quotes.text: After nearly two decades of steady declines, Mexico’s petroleum and liquid fuels production has remained stable since 2019, and we forecast production in Mexico will remain relatively flat through 2024. Private companies have increased petroleum production in Mexico over the past five years. In 2022, Mexican government data show that private production contributed more than 5% of Mexico’s total, a large increase from the 0.5% oil contribution that private companies produced in 2016.

Mexico’s forecast liquid fuels production averages 1.9 million b/d in 2021, almost unchanged from 2019 and 2020. We have revised our 2021 production forecast upwards from its January 2021 STEO estimate of 1.8 million b/d because private operators have surpassed our expectations regarding their ability to ramp up the Ixachi, Pokoch, and Hokchi fields.

Several dynamics have led to production stability. For example, decreasing production of the historically top-producing shallow-water fields of the Sureste Basin (formerly known as the Campeche Basin) on the southeastern coast of Mexico has been replaced by recent field developments in other sections of the Sureste Basin, such as the 133,000 b/d from the Quesqui field in 2022, according to our updated Country Analysis Brief: Mexico

reasons: Eligible evidence supports a private-production contribution, without establishing exclusive causation or an ownership-based decomposition.
The expanded forecast quote supplies the 1.9 million b/d value omitted from both originals’ quoted excerpts.

question: How much did Argentina’s crude-oil production change from January 2021 through September 2024, and what roles did Vaca Muerta and conventional fields play in that change?

answer_points.text: Argentina's crude-oil production increased 50% from January 2021 through September 2024; rising Vaca Muerta shale output drove the increase and offset declining conventional-field output.
In September 2024, national crude production averaged 738,000 b/d, its highest monthly level since 2003, with Vaca Muerta accounting for 58%.

quotes.text: Crude oil and natural gas production in Argentina are both nearing record highs, driven by increasing output from the Vaca Muerta shale formation , which is offsetting declining output from conventional oil and natural gas fields. From January 2021 through September 2024, crude oil production in Argentina increased by 50%, and natural gas production rose by 27%, lifting output of both fuels near the records set in the early 2000s

In September 2024, production averaged 738,000 barrels per day (b/d) of crude oil in Argentina, 15% more than in September 2023 and the most in any month since 2003. In September, oil produced in the Vaca Muerta formation accounted for 58% of the country’s total output

reasons: Cutoff-eligible evidence directly gives the requested crude-oil change and distinguishes shale growth from conventional declines.

question: How did OPEC+ announcements about planned production increases during 2024 contrast with reported production developments in the United States, Guyana and Canada, and what did EIA report about their offsetting supply effects?

answer_points.text: OPEC+ repeatedly announced delays to planned production increases during 2024, while non-OPEC+ production continued growing and offset OPEC+ cuts.
U.S. crude production reached a monthly record of 13.5 million b/d in October 2024; Guyana and Canada also increased production on an annual basis in 2024.

quotes.text: OPEC+ announced delays to production increases multiple times in 2024. However, production growth from non-OPEC+ members continued to increase, offsetting OPEC+ production cuts.
U.S. production of crude oil reached a monthly record in October 2024 of 13.5 million b/d, and production in Guyana and Canada also increased on an annual basis in 2024.

reasons: The January 17 retrospective directly contrasts announcements with reported production; earlier forecasts are background and later estimates are ineligible.

question: How much crude oil did Saudi Arabia burn for electricity generation in 2017, and what role were the Wasit, Hasbah and Arabiyah gas developments expected to play in its longer-term power-generation fuel mix as of May 2018?

answer_points.text: Saudi Arabia burned nearly 0.5 million b/d of crude oil for electricity generation in 2017.
As of May 2018, continued development of Wasit, Hasbah and Arabiyah natural gas fields was expected to reduce long-term reliance on crude oil for power generation.

quotes.text: the country burned nearly 0.5 million b/d of crude oil for electricity generation in 2017.
The continued development of the Wasit, Hasbah, and Arabiyah natural gas fields is expected to reduce the country’s long-term reliance on power generation from crude oil.

reasons: May 2018 evidence supplies the observed 2017 burn and separately states the expected long-term role of gas developments.

question: Does EIA’s May 2019 analysis of 43 publicly reporting U.S. oil producers establish that lower production costs per barrel of oil equivalent characterized the U.S. oil-producing industry as a whole in 2018?

answer_points.text: No. The 43 publicly reporting producers were selected for data availability, not statistical representativeness, and EIA explicitly said their results need not represent the whole U.S. oil-production industry.
The companies accounted for about one-third of U.S. crude oil and natural gas liquids production in fourth-quarter 2018; the lower-cost finding applies to that analyzed group.

Cost definitions and comparison periods matter: direct upstream expenses rose 16% from 2017 to $24/BOE in 2018, while expenses including depreciation, impairments and other costs averaged $48/BOE, the lowest during 2013–2018.

quotes.text: However, these companies were not selected as a statistically representative sample but instead because their results are publically available. Their results do not necessarily represent the U.S. oil production industry as a whole.
EIA calculates that these companies accounted for about one-third of total U.S. crude oil and natural gas liquids production in the fourth quarter of 2018.

Lower production costs per barrel of oil equivalent (BOE) and increased production levels contributed to a higher return on equity for these companies for the fourth quarter of 2018 than in any quarter from 2013 through 2018.

expenses directly related to upstream production activities increased 16% between 2017 and 2018 to $24/BOE. When including depreciation, impairments , and other costs not directly related to upstream production, expenses for these 43 companies averaged $48/BOE in 2018, the lowest amount from 2013 to 2018.

reasons: The evidence sufficiently answers the inference question negatively through an explicit sampling limitation; it does not establish industry-wide costs.

question: How severe was the decline in U.S. kerosene-type jet-fuel exports in the first half of 2020 relative to the same period in 2019, and when did exports reach their monthly trough?

answer_points.text: First-half 2020 U.S. kerosene-type jet-fuel exports averaged 134,000 b/d, down 71,000 b/d (35%) from first-half 2019.
Exports reached their monthly trough in May 2020 at 23,000 b/d, the lowest since mid-2007.

quotes.text: In the first half of 2020, the United States exported 134,000 b/d of kerosene-type jet fuel, a 71,000 b/d (35%) decrease from the same period in 2019. U.S. jet fuel exports hit a low point in May, falling to just 23,000 b/d, their lowest value since mid-2007.

reasons: Eligible evidence directly reports both the half-year decline and monthly trough; later full-year figures are excluded.

question: As of September 2023, how were Saudi Arabian production cuts and new Middle East refinery demand affecting the supply-demand balance for sour crude relative to sweet crude?

answer_points.text: Saudi and broader OPEC+ cuts tightened medium and heavy sour crude supply and raised sour prices more than sweet prices.
Higher Saudi official selling prices and heightened demand as new Middle East refineries came online further supported sour crude prices, narrowing sweet–sour spreads.
Further demand growth remained prospective: Duqm was scheduled for completion by end-2023, while Al Zour was operating at 410,000 b/d with a 615,000 b/d year-end capacity target.

quotes.text: Production cuts among OPEC+ members are limiting availability of medium and heavy sour grades of crude oil and contributing to higher relative prices for these grades, reversing typical price relationships.
The production cuts are having a larger impact on the price of sour crude oils

Saudi Arabia also increased the official selling price (OSP) of Arab Light (a medium, sour crude oil) to Asia and Europe, further pushing up sour crude oil prices. As a result, sweet and sour crude oil price spreads have narrowed in most major trading hubs
heightened demand for sour crude oil as several new Middle East refineries come online.

In Oman, the 230,000 b/d Duqm refinery (a joint venture between Oman’s OQ Group and Kuwait Petroleum International) is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2023 and its feedstock is mainly sour and heavy crude oils. Kuwait’s Al Zour refinery is currently operating at 410,000 b/d , with a target capacity of 615,000 b/d by the end of 2023

reasons: Eligible September reports directly describe relative supply tightening, refinery demand, and observed price effects; future refinery targets are distinguished from operating throughput.

question: How much did Lower 48 production of crude oil with API gravity between 30.1 and 40.0 degrees grow in January–October 2023 compared with the same period in 2022, and what monthly production record did this grade range reach?

answer_points.text: Lower 48 production in the 30.1–40.0 degree API range grew 19% in January–October 2023 versus the same period in 2022.
Production in that range reached a monthly record of 4.75 million b/d in September 2023.

quotes.text: Overall in the Lower 48 states, 19% more crude oil with an API gravity between 30.1 and 40.0 degrees was produced in the first 10 months of 2023 than during the same period in 2022.
In September 2023, Lower 48 crude oil production in this API gravity range established a new record of 4.75 million b/d.

reasons: The cutoff-day publication supplies both the exact comparative growth and monthly record.

question: Does the evidence available by April 16, 2025 establish how much of the Permian region's 2024 crude oil production growth was attributable specifically to artificial intelligence, separately from other productivity improvements?

answer_points.text: Permian crude production rose 370,000 b/d in 2024 to average 6.3 million b/d, despite 26 fewer active rigs than in 2023.

The evidence attributes growth to improved well productivity and lists AI alongside electronic hydraulic fracturing and automated drilling; it does not isolate an AI-specific volume or share of growth.

quotes.text: Permian region production also accounted for almost all the growth in 2024, rising by 370,000 b/d compared with 2023 to average 6.3 million b/d.
The Permian region averaged 308 active drilling rigs in 2024, accounting for more than half of the rigs in operation last year but 26 fewer rigs than in 2023.

Even with the lower rig count in 2024, Permian production grew because well productivity improved . Producers used technological advancements such as artificial intelligence, electronic hydraulic fracturing technology, and automated drilling processes to optimize operations.

reasons: Total growth and a qualitative technology explanation are supported, but no eligible passage quantifies AI's separate contribution. Later sources are excluded.

question: Does the evidence establishing U.S. leadership in petroleum and natural gas hydrocarbon production in 2017 also establish that the United States was the largest producer of crude oil alone that year?

answer_points.text: No: the leadership statement concerns petroleum and natural gas hydrocarbons, with petroleum encompassing multiple liquid fuels, rather than crude oil alone.

Crude oil and lease condensate accounted for only 60% of U.S. petroleum hydrocarbon production in 2017; natural gas plant liquids accounted for 24%, so the broader leadership claim does not establish a crude-only ranking.

quotes.text: The United States remained the world's top producer of petroleum and natural gas hydrocarbons in 2017, reaching a record high.
Total petroleum production is made up of several different types of liquid fuels, including crude oil and lease condensate, tight oil, extra-heavy oil, and bitumen.
In the United States, crude oil and lease condensate accounted for 60% of total petroleum hydrocarbon production in 2017, and natural gas plant liquids accounted for 24%.

reasons: The eligible evidence establishes the scope mismatch. It does not provide a comparative 2017 crude-only ranking, and later ranking reports cannot resolve that historical question at this cutoff.

question: During the California refinery outages and inventory drawdowns reported in May 2019, what constrained gasoline resupply from elsewhere in the United States, and which overseas refining regions provided alternative supply?

answer_points.text: Geographic isolation and limited petroleum infrastructure connections to the rest of the United States constrained West Coast resupply; California's different gasoline specifications further restricted options.
After regional inventory drawdowns, alternative resupply came through imports from refineries in Asia or Europe, a costly option.

quotes.text: The West Coast is isolated by both geography and a lack of petroleum infrastructure connections to the rest of the United States. In addition, California requires a different gasoline specification than the rest of the country, further narrowing resupply options.
These restrictions mean that after drawing down in-region inventories, the next available resupply is through imports from refineries in Asia or Europe
This method of resupply is costly, and wholesale prices in the region have increased to cover these associated costs.

reasons: Eligible May reports directly identify both domestic resupply constraints and overseas refining regions.

question: Between 2005 and 2019, how did Canada's share and volume of U.S. crude oil imports change relative to the change in total U.S. crude oil imports?

answer_points.text: Canada's share of U.S. crude imports rose from within the reported 12%–16% range in 2005 to 56% in 2019; Canadian volume more than doubled to 3.8 million b/d.
Total U.S. crude imports moved in the opposite direction, falling from more than 10.1 million b/d in 2005 to 6.8 million b/d in 2019, about one-third lower.

quotes.text: In 2005, U.S. refineries relied heavily on foreign crude oil, importing a record volume of more than 10.1 million barrels per day (b/d). About 60% of the imported crude oil came from four countries: Canada, Mexico, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela, and each was responsible for between 12% and 16% of total U.S. crude oil imports that year.
In total, U.S. crude oil imports have fallen sharply, but imports from Canada have risen steadily to 3.8 million b/d, more than twice the imports from Canada in 2005.
U.S. crude oil imports from Canada accounted for 56% of all U.S. crude oil imports in 2019
As a result, by 2019, total U.S. crude oil imports were down to 6.8 million b/d, or about one-third less than 2005 volumes.

reasons: The direct comparison is supported. The source gives a range rather than an exact Canada-specific 2005 share or volume, so no exact baseline is invented.

question: How did Texas and New Mexico compare in net additions to proved crude oil reserves in 2017, and what roles did crude prices and Permian Basin development play in those additions?

question: How did EIA adapt its assessment of non-U.S. oil consumption during 2020 beyond its usual GDP-based modeling, and which additional indicators did it use?

question: How did Mexico's petroleum and liquid fuels production-consumption balance evolve from 2019 through the end of 2022, and what role did the 2020 demand contraction play in its net-importer status?

quotes.text: In the week ending November 1, 2024, inventories decreased to slightly more than 100 million barrels, about 11% more than the five-year average.

U.S. propane inventories grew 94% since the start of the storage injection season (the week ending April 5, 2024). Last year, propane inventories grew 77% from the first week of April to 98 million barrels for the week ending November 3, 2023.

reasons: The cutoff-date source gives both comparable seasonal growth rates and ending stocks. The 17-point difference is calculated from 94% minus 77%.

question: How did 2024 changes in crude oil production and average rig counts compare between the Eagle Ford and Bakken regions?

answer_points.text: In 2024, Eagle Ford and Bakken crude production each increased by 13,000 b/d to about 1.2 million b/d, remaining mostly flat overall.
Eagle Ford's average rig count fell by 9 to 54, whereas Bakken's fell by 2 to 34; Eagle Ford had the larger rig reduction despite the same production increase.

quotes.text: Both Eagle Ford and Bakken production showed similar growth, rising by 13,000 b/d to 1.2 million b/d. The rig count in the Eagle Ford fell by 9 rigs in 2024 to average 54 rigs, while the rig count in the Bakken fell by 2 rigs to average 34 rigs in 2024.

reasons: The April 16 source directly reports annual production changes and average rig counts for both regions.

question: As of April 4, 2018, how had annual average U.S. crude oil production changed in 2016 and 2017, and what annual average levels did EIA project for 2018 and 2019?

answer_points.text: Annual average U.S. crude production fell by 551,000 b/d in 2016, then increased by 464,000 b/d in 2017 to 9.3 million b/d.
As of April 4, 2018, EIA projected annual average crude production of 10.7 million b/d in 2018 and 11.3 million b/d in 2019.

quotes.text: Annual average U.S. crude oil production reached 9.3 million barrels per day (b/d) in 2017, an increase of 464,000 b/d from 2016 levels after declining by 551,000 b/d in 2016.
EIA projects that U.S. crude oil production will continue to grow in 2018 and 2019 , averaging 10.7 million b/d and 11.3 million b/d, respectively.

reasons: The April 4 source provides historical changes and the then-current forecast. The earlier March report gives a slightly different 2017 increase of 463,000 b/d; later revisions are excluded.

question: What role did new projects and expansions play in Federal Gulf of Mexico crude oil production growth in 2018, and how did the number of projects brought online that year compare with expected 2019 starts as of April 2019?

answer_points.text: New projects and expansions started since 2016 contributed to Federal Gulf of Mexico production growth in 2018, when production increased by 61,000 b/d to a record annual average of 1.74 million b/d.
Producers brought 11 new projects online in 2018; as of April 9, 2019, another 8 were expected in 2019, three fewer than the 2018 starts.

quotes.text: In the Federal Gulf of Mexico, new projects and expansions that have started since 2016 have contributed to the growth in production in 2018. Oil and natural gas producers brought online 11 new projects in 2018, and 8 more are expected to come online in 2019. The Federal Gulf of Mexico’s crude oil production grew by 61,000 b/d, leading to its highest annual average of 1.74 million b/d.

reasons: The April 9 report directly answers the question, distinguishing realized 2018 starts from expected 2019 starts. It does not attribute the entire production increase exclusively to new projects.

question: Which fuel component and supplying country drove the reversal in U.S. biomass-based diesel imports in 2019, and how large was the aggregate increase in percentage terms and the resulting volume in barrels per day?

answer_points.text: Higher renewable diesel imports from Singapore drove the reversal: aggregate U.S. biomass-based diesel imports rose 26% in 2019 to more than 27,000 b/d.

quotes.text: U.S. imports of biomass-based diesel, which include biodiesel and renewable diesel, grew 26% in 2019 to more than 27,000 barrels per day (b/d), reversing three years of decline. Imports of biomass-based diesel increased in 2019 because of the increase in renewable diesel imports from Singapore.

reasons: The cutoff-date report directly identifies the component, supplier, percentage growth, and gross import volume; net-import forecasts are distinct.

question: How severe was the U.S. petroleum products consumption contraction in 2020 in terms of total barrels per day and historical standing, and how broadly did the decline extend across sectors, including transportation?

answer_points.text: U.S. petroleum products consumption fell to 18.1 million b/d in 2020, a 25-year low.
Consumption declined in every energy-consuming sector from 2019 to 2020, with transportation recording a record 15% decrease.

quotes.text: In 2020, 18.1 million barrels per day (b/d) of petroleum products were consumed in the United States, a 25-year low. From 2019 to 2020, petroleum consumption decreased in every energy-consuming sector, and it decreased a record 15% in the transportation sector.

reasons: The cutoff-date annual report directly supplies the consumption level, historical standing, and sector breadth. The 18.1 million b/d figure is the resulting consumption level, not the size of the decline.

question: Does evidence available by September 26, 2023 establish that KNPC's Clean Fuels Project alone caused Kuwait's crude oil export decline from the 2022 average to the first seven months of 2023?

answer_points.text: The report records crude exports falling from 1.9 million b/d in 2022 to less than 1.8 million b/d in the first seven months of 2023, and says the Clean Fuels Project added around 60,000 b/d of refining capacity; this does not establish sole causation.

The evidence attributes Kuwait's broader refining capacity increase to both Al Zour and expansions at existing refineries, so it does not isolate the Clean Fuels Project as the sole cause of the export shift.

The pool also reports Kuwait's pledged production cut of 128,000 b/d for May–December 2023 and forecasts lower annual production, providing another relevant supply consideration without measuring its contribution to the export decline.

quotes.text: The CFP increased Kuwait’s crude oil refining capacity by around 60,000 b/d. Kuwait’s crude oil exports fell from an average of 1.9 million b/d in 2022 to less than 1.8 million b/d for the first 7 months of 2023.
The increase in capacity comes from the new Al Zour refinery and an expansion project at existing refineries over the past two years.

Kuwait pledged to cut its production by 128,000 b/d during this time, which lowered its monthly production target to below 2.6 million b/d.16 We forecast that Kuwait’s overall 2023 oil production will decline slightly compared with the 2022 averages because of this voluntary reduction.

reasons: No: the pool establishes the export decline and multiple relevant developments, but supplies no causal decomposition or evidence that the Clean Fuels Project alone caused it. This suffices to answer the evidentiary question negatively.

question: Between the 2023 average and January–May 2024, how did Saudi and Iraqi crude shipments to Europe compare with Asian and Middle Eastern oil product shipments to Europe in their contributions to increased flows around the Cape of Good Hope, using data with May still preliminary?

answer_points.text: With May 2024 preliminary, Saudi and Iraqi crude shipments westbound to Europe accounted for 15% of the increase in Cape flows, versus 29% from Asian and Middle Eastern oil product exports to Europe—14 percentage points more, or nearly twice the contribution.

quotes.text: May 2024 is preliminary data.

Middle Eastern crude oil producers Saudi Arabia and Iraq sent more crude oil around the cape westbound to Europe than through the Suez Canal, which is accessed by the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb to the south. This increase in trade flow volume made up 15% of the total increase between the average of 2023 and January through May of 2024. Asian and Middle Eastern refiners increased their oil product exports to Europe and diverted cargoes westbound around the cape, representing 29% of the increased trade around the cape.

reasons: The eligible body directly supplies both contributions, the comparison periods, and the preliminary-data qualification.

question: From Canada's start of waterborne propane exports in 2019 through 2024, how did export growth toward Asia compare with the U.S. import trend, and how did the principal uses of Canadian propane differ between East Asia and the United States?

answer_points.text: Canadian propane exports expanded toward Asia and reached record overall levels in 2024, while U.S. imports from Canada stayed relatively consistent since waterborne exports began in 2019; the United States accounted for 58% of Canadian exports in 2024.

Canadian propane sent to East Asia was mostly petrochemical feedstock, whereas exports to the United States were mostly for space heating, particularly in the Upper Midwest and Northeast during winter.

quotes.text: Canada’s propane exports have steadily increased over the last decade, reaching record highs in 2024 as new marine export terminals streamlined the flow of propane from western Canada to export destinations, particularly to Asia. U.S. propane imports from Canada have stayed relatively consistent since Canada began waterborne exports in 2019.
Although the United States is still the largest destination for the country’s propane exports, it accounted for just 58% of exports in 2024 as shipments to Asia have risen sharply.

Most propane exported from Canada to East Asia is consumed as petrochemical feedstock, while propane exported from Canada to the United States is used mostly for space-heating demand, particularly in the Upper-Midwest and Northeast during the winter.

reasons: Eligible retrospective evidence directly establishes the contrasting export trends and principal uses.

question: What product-level changes kept U.S. petroleum product exports growing in the first half of 2019 relative to the first half of 2018, and what factors did EIA identify as likely restraining overall export growth?

answer_points.text: Petroleum product exports increased by 19,000 b/d (0.3%) to 5.47 million b/d in first-half 2019, as propane and distillate increases offset declines in all other products.
Propane exports increased by 142,000 b/d (16%) to 1.03 million b/d, while distillate increased by 60,000 b/d (5%) to 1.3 million b/d.

Residual fuel exports had the largest decline, falling 74,000 b/d to 258,000 b/d; exports to Singapore fell 68,000 b/d as its bunker market drew down higher-sulfur inventories ahead of new marine-fuel rules.
EIA identified lower refinery runs and slowing global economic growth limiting petroleum product demand as likely restraints on exports.

quotes.text: In the first half of 2019, the United States exported 5.47 million barrels per day (b/d) of petroleum products, an increase of 19,000 b/d (0.3%) from the first half of 2018 and the slowest year-over-year growth rate for any half year in 13 years.

Lower U.S. refinery runs in the first half of 2019 compared with the first half of 2018 and slowing global economic growth , which is limiting demand for petroleum products, likely contributed to lower exports. In the first half of 2019, increased exports of propane and distillate offset decreased exports of all other petroleum products (Figure 1).
Distillate remained the top petroleum product export by volume in the first half of 2019, averaging 1.3 million b/d, an increase of 60,000 b/d (5%) compared with the first half of 2018.
Propane was the second-largest U.S. petroleum product export in the first half of 2019 at 1.03 million b/d, which is an increase of 142,000 b/d (16%) from the first half of 2018.
U.S. residual fuel exports declined the most between the first half of 2019 and the first half of 2018, falling by 74,000 b/d to average 258,000 b/d.

However, in the first half of 2019, trade press reported that Singapore’s bunker market was preparing for new international regulations that limit the sulfur content of marine fuels by drawing down higher sulfur residual inventories to make room for inventories that are lower in sulfur. As a result, average U.S. exports of residual fuel oil to Singapore decreased 68,000 b/d (80%) in the first half of 2019 compared with the first half of 2018.

reasons: Contemporaneous passages provide the product offsets and explicitly qualified explanations for restrained growth; later evidence is excluded.

question: Why did EIA's January 2020 outlook project Federal Offshore Gulf of Mexico crude oil production growth in 2020 but relatively flat production in 2021 despite expected new project starts?

answer_points.text: EIA forecast Gulf of Mexico crude production to increase by 0.1 million b/d to 2.0 million b/d in 2020, then remain relatively flat in 2021 because several new projects would start only late in 2021 and their contributions would be offset by declines at existing fields.

quotes.text: EIA forecasts that production from the Federal Offshore Gulf of Mexico will grow by 0.1 million b/d in 2020 to 2.0 million b/d and to remain relatively flat in 2021 because several projects expected to come online in 2021 will not start producing until late in the year and will be offset by declines from other producing fields.

reasons: The January outlook directly explains the forecast profile; these are projections, not realized production or project starts.

question: How did the Magellan East Houston–Brent spread help EIA assess geographic and logistical explanations versus sweet–sour supply and demand explanations for the widening Mars–Brent discount in 2021?

answer_points.text: Because MEH and Brent are both light, sweet crude oils of similar quality, EIA used their spread to assess geographic and logistical influences on Gulf Coast prices relative to Brent.
The MEH–Brent spread narrowed to -$0.80/b in November to date from -$1.71/b in August and -$0.87/b in January, suggesting geographic factors were not driving the widening Mars–Brent discount.
Mars's November discount to Brent averaged $4.92/b versus $4.09/b in August and $1.47/b in January; EIA considered differences in sweet–sour supply and demand the likely explanation.
The sweet–sour explanation combined increasing supplies of sour OPEC grades with higher natural gas treatment costs that made sour crude less economical for refiners.

quotes.text: Magellan East Houston and Brent are both light, sweet crude oils of similar quality, and therefore, the Magellan East Houston-Brent spread reflects how geographic and logistical factors affect U.S. Gulf Coast crude oil prices relative to Brent prices. Differences in supply and demand for sweet versus sour crude oils likely explain the increasing discount between Mars crude oil and Brent crude oil.

The MEH-Brent spread has averaged -$0.80/b so far in November, narrower than the average of -$1.71/b in August and -$0.87/b in January. This price increase for the light, sweet MEH crude oil relative to Brent crude oil prices indicates that geographic factors have likely not contributed to the wider price spreads that have occurred between the sourer Mars crude oil and Brent.

The Mars crude oil spot price averaged $4.92 per barrel (b) less than the Brent crude oil spot price in November. This price spread is higher than the $4.09/b average price difference between Mars and Brent crude oil in August (the first month of recently announced production increases from OPEC+ ). The spread is also significantly higher than the $1.47/b average spot price difference between Mars and Brent crude oil in January.

One contributing factor to the widening spread between sweet and sour crude oils is the increasing supply of medium and heavy sour crude oils. OPEC has been increasing production and exports since the second half of 2021, particularly in countries that produce sour grades.

Higher treatment costs of sour crude oil have likely made them less economic for refiners as global natural gas prices have increased, contributing to higher demand for sweeter crude (lower sulfur) oils such as Magellan East Houston (MEH) and lower demand for more sour crude oils, such as Mars.

reasons: The evidence provides the quality-controlled comparison and the alternative supply-demand explanation, while distinguishing November-to-date from full-November averages.

question: How did the average Dated Brent–Dubai Fateh price relationship change between January 4, 2021–June 20, 2023 and June 21–September 19, 2023, and how did EIA relate that change to OPEC+ cuts affecting sour crude supply?

answer_points.text: Dated Brent averaged a $2.56/b premium over Dubai Fateh during January 4, 2021–June 20, 2023; during June 21–September 19, 2023, Dubai instead averaged a $0.48/b premium, a $3.04/b shift toward Dubai.

EIA attributed the reversal to OPEC+ cuts limiting medium and heavy sour crude supplies, raising their prices relative to sweet crude, which typically commands a premium because it costs less to refine and yields more valuable products.

quotes.text: Dated Brent traded at an average premium of $2.56 per barrel (b) compared with Dubai Fateh between January 4, 2021, and June 20, 2023. However, between June 21 and September 19, the roles reversed, and Dubai Fateh traded at an average premium of $0.48/b compared with Dated Brent.

Crude oil production cuts among OPEC+ members are limiting the global supply of medium, sour and heavy, sour grades of crude oil. These cuts are increasing prices for these grades compared with sweet crude oils, reversing typical price relationships.
Light, sweet crude oils typically trade at a premium compared with any sour crude oil because sweet crude oils cost less to refine and produce higher yields of more valuable products.

reasons: The cutoff-eligible passage gives both exact averaging windows and EIA's supply explanation.

question: Does the reported 2023 increase in combined proved crude oil and natural gas reserves for EIA's sample of 175 publicly traded exploration and production companies establish that those companies added crude oil reserves through new discoveries?

answer_points.text: No. The reported 2023 increase was 2.0 billion BOE, about 1%, in combined proved crude oil and natural gas reserves for 175 companies; that aggregate does not isolate crude oil additions from new discoveries.

Reserves can change through price- and information-driven revisions, extensions and discoveries, asset purchases and sales, and production; therefore a net reserve increase cannot by itself establish new crude oil discoveries.

quotes.text: Global proved crude oil and natural gas reserves held by 175 publicly traded global exploration and production (E&P) companies increased by 2.0 billion barrels of oil equivalent (BOE) in 2023, or about 1%, according to data from the companies’ annual financial reports.

Company assessments of their proved reserves of crude oil and natural gas change from year to year because of: Revisions to existing reserves driven by prices and new information from drilling Extensions and discoveries of new resources Purchases and sales of proved reserves Production

Proved reserves acquired through purchases and sales represent transfers of assets between companies, including companies outside of this analysis. Revisions to proved reserves can be affected by changes in crude oil and natural gas prices and are less directly affected by E&D investment.

reasons: The evidence sufficiently supports rejecting the proposed inference, without establishing whether particular crude discoveries occurred.

question: How large was the increase in annual average U.S. crude oil production in 2024, what level did production reach, and how concentrated was the growth in the Permian region?

answer_points.text: EIA's January 2025 estimate put annual average U.S. crude oil production at a record 13.2 million b/d in 2024.
The Permian accounted for almost all 2024 production growth: its annual average increased 370,000 b/d to 6.3 million b/d, representing 48% of total U.S. crude oil production.

quotes.text: We estimate U.S. crude oil production set a record of 13.2 million barrels per day (b/d) in 2024.

In 2024, the Permian region in western Texas and southeastern New Mexico produced more crude oil than any other region, accounting for 48% of total U.S. crude oil production. Permian region production also accounted for almost all the growth in 2024, rising by 370,000 b/d compared with 2023 to average 6.3 million b/d.

reasons: Eligible bodies establish the national level and Permian contribution, but do not give the realized national annual increase. The 2% body figure is a June 2024 forecast; the retrospective 2% appears only in title metadata and cannot supply that missing fact.

question: Which regional markets and countries were prominent destinations for U.S. crude oil exports in the first half of 2018, and which major destination differed from the broader growth trend relative to the first half of 2017?

answer_points.text: Asia and Oceania were the largest regional recipients in first-half 2018. Exports to China more than doubled, increasing 193,000 b/d from first-half 2017; South Korea and India increased by 81,000 and 72,000 b/d, respectively.
Europe was the second-largest market at 555,000 b/d, with Italy, the United Kingdom, and the Netherlands each receiving more than 120,000 b/d.
Canada was the only major destination with declining exports, down 13,000 b/d compared with first-half 2017.

quotes.text: Destinations in Asia and Oceania were the largest recipients of U.S. crude oil exports in the first half of 2018, and U.S. crude oil exports to China more than doubled—increasing by 193,000 b/d—from the first half of 2017. U.S. crude oil exports to South Korea and India also increased significantly during this period, up 81,000 b/d and 72,000 b/d, respectively.

Europe was the second-largest market for U.S. crude oil exports, receiving 555,000 b/d in the first half of 2018. U.S. crude oil export volumes to Europe are more equally distributed than in other regions. Italy, the United Kingdom, and the Netherlands, each received more than 120,000 b/d in the first half of 2018.
Canada was the only major U.S. crude oil export destination where exports decreased somewhat, down 13,000 b/d in the first half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017 (Figure 2).

reasons: Eligible contemporary bodies identify both leading regions, prominent countries, and the exception to growth.

question: How did U.S. Gulf Coast gross crude oil imports in December 2018 compare with December 2013, and how did OPEC-origin imports in December 2018 compare with their first-half 2018 average, in million barrels per day?

answer_points.text: Gulf Coast gross crude oil imports were 1.9 million b/d in December 2018 versus 3.7 million b/d in December 2013, a decline of 1.8 million b/d.
OPEC-origin Gulf Coast crude imports were 1.1 million b/d in December 2018 versus a first-half 2018 average of 1.5 million b/d, a decline of 0.4 million b/d.

quotes.text: In addition, Gulf Coast gross crude oil imports reached record lows in the final months of 2018, with imports of 1.9 million b/d in December compared with 3.7 million b/d at the same time five years ago.

In particular, Gulf Coast crude oil imports from members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) fell sharply in the final two months of 2018, from an average of 1.5 million b/d in the first half of 2018 to 1.1 million b/d in December.

reasons: The cutoff-date source directly provides both gross-import comparisons; differences are simple subtraction in million b/d.

question: In EIA's July 2020 outlook, what was the observed April trough in U.S. liquid fuels consumption measured by product supplied, and how long was total petroleum and other liquid fuels consumption forecast to remain below the 2019 average?

answer_points.text: April 2020 U.S. liquid fuels consumption, measured by product supplied, reached 14.7 million b/d, its lowest monthly level since the early 1980s.
EIA forecast total petroleum and other liquid fuels consumption to remain below the 2019 average until August 2021.

quotes.text: levels will remain lower than the 2019 average until August 2021.

In April, consumption of liquid fuels in the United States (as measured by product supplied) reached its all-time monthly low since the early 1980s at an average of 14.7 million barrels per day (b/d).

reasons: The cutoff-eligible July account directly supplies both the observed trough and the forecast horizon; the forecast does not establish realized recovery.

question: How did EIA's February 2021 forecasts for U.S. net crude oil imports and net petroleum product exports combine to imply a return to net petroleum imports in 2021 and 2022, compared with 2020?

answer_points.text: In 2020, crude oil net imports averaged 2.7 million b/d and petroleum product net exports averaged 3.4 million b/d, implying approximately 0.7 million b/d of net petroleum exports.

For 2021, forecast crude net imports of 3.7 million b/d exceeded product net exports of 3.5 million b/d; for 2022, 4.4 million b/d exceeded 3.9 million b/d. The rounded components imply net petroleum imports of approximately 0.2 and 0.5 million b/d, respectively.
EIA explicitly forecast net petroleum imports of 230,000 b/d in 2021 and 550,000 b/d in 2022, reversing 2020's annual net-export position.
EIA expected increasing refinery crude requirements to outstrip domestic production and inventory draws, raising crude imports enough to reverse the overall petroleum trade balance.

quotes.text: EIA forecasts that net imports of crude oil will increase from its 2020 average of 2.7 million barrels per day (b/d) to 3.7 million b/d in 2021 and 4.4 million b/d in 2022.

On an annual average basis, U.S. net petroleum product exports—distillate fuel oil, hydrocarbon gas liquids, and motor gasoline, among others—averaged 3.2 million b/d in 2019 and 3.4 million b/d in 2020. EIA forecasts that net petroleum product exports will average 3.5 million b/d in 2021 and 3.9 million b/d in 2022
In 2021 and 2022, EIA expects the United States to return to being a net petroleum importer, averaging 230,000 b/d in 2021 and 550,000 b/d in 2022.
EIA forecasts increases in net crude oil imports in 2021 and 2022 because domestic crude oil production and inventory draws alone will not meet the needs of U.S. refineries

reasons: February sources provide both trade components and explicit net forecasts. Arithmetic using rounded components differs slightly from the explicitly reported net forecasts; future balances remain forecasts.

question: In EIA's High Oil Price case described in April 2023, what mechanism was projected to reverse initial U.S. crude oil production growth after 2030, and how did that mechanism affect petroleum and other liquids production through 2050?

answer_points.text: In the High Oil Price case, initially rapid crude production growth reverses after 2030 because increasingly close well spacing reduces productivity until new drilling becomes unprofitable and stops.
The resulting lack of new drilling reduces petroleum and other liquids production between 2030 and 2050, although projected 2050 production remains 27% above 2022.

quotes.text: However, crude oil production begins to fall after 2030 because wells are drilled increasingly close to one another, resulting in less well productivity. Eventually this trend becomes unprofitable, at which point new drilling stops.

Because of the lack of new drilling, petroleum and other liquids production decreases between 2030 and 2050. By 2050, we project in the High Oil Price case that production increases by 27% compared with 2022

reasons: The April 2023 body directly explains the projected mechanism and outcome. Decline from 2030 is compatible with remaining above the 2022 baseline.

question: As of May 21, 2024, which floating production, storage, and offloading vessels supported Guyana's oil production, and which projects did that fleet serve?

answer_points.text: Guyana's producing FPSO fleet comprised Liza Destiny, Liza Unity, and Prosperity, collectively serving the Liza and Payara projects.

quotes.text: Guyana's oil production comes from three floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessels : Liza Destiny, Liza Unity, and Prosperity. These vessels produce oil and natural gas from the Liza and Payara projects.

reasons: The May 21 body explicitly names all three operating vessels and their collective projects. Later fleet developments are cutoff-ineligible.

question: How high was U.S. propane consumption measured as product supplied in January 2025, how did it rank against previous January and all-month observations, and what demand driver did EIA identify?

answer_points.text: January 2025 U.S. propane consumption, measured as product supplied, was 1.48 million b/d—the highest January consumption since January 2005 and highest monthly consumption since February 2007.
EIA attributed the increase to severe cold raising space-heating demand; January 2025 was the coldest U.S. month since January 2014 when measured by heating degree days.

quotes.text: U.S. propane consumption reached 1.48 million barrels per day (b/d) in January 2025, the most January consumption on record since January 2005 and the most for any month since February 2007, as severe cold drove up heating demand across much of the country.
U.S. propane consumption, which we measure as product supplied , is closely correlated with temperatures during the winter because propane is primarily used for space heating in the United States.
January 2025 was the coldest month recorded in the United States since January 2014, measured by heating degree days (HDDs).

reasons: The cutoff-day publication directly reports the January observation, historical comparisons, measurement, and demand driver.

question: Does the near-flat U.S. crude oil and lease condensate proved-reserve balance between year-end 2015 and year-end 2016 establish that new discoveries alone replaced the reserves depleted by production?

answer_points.text: No. Crude oil and lease condensate proved reserves remained virtually unchanged at 35.2 billion barrels, but that net balance does not establish that new discoveries alone replaced production depletion.

EIA states that annual reserve changes include discoveries, extensions, net revisions and other adjustments, and production reductions; the near-flat total does not isolate the contribution from discoveries.

quotes.text: U.S. crude oil and lease condensate proved reserves remained virtually unchanged from their 2015 level, at 35.2 billion barrels.

Changes in proved reserves from year to year reflect new discoveries, either in new fields, new reservoirs in old fields, or extensions of existing reservoirs; net revisions and other adjustments to previous reserve estimates; and reductions from annual production of each fuel.

reasons: The evidence suffices to reject the proposed inference. It does not quantify a discoveries-only replacement rate, but that is unnecessary to answer whether the net balance establishes one.

question: In EIA's AEO2019 Reference case, how does the combined projected share of cumulative U.S. tight oil production through 2050 from the Spraberry, Bone Spring, and Wolfcamp compare with the shares from the Bakken and Eagle Ford?

answer_points.text: The Spraberry, Bone Spring, and Wolfcamp together were projected to supply approximately half of cumulative U.S. tight oil production through 2050, versus 19% from the Bakken and 17% from the Eagle Ford.
The three Permian plays' approximately 50% share exceeds the Bakken and Eagle Ford combined share of 36% by approximately 14 percentage points.

quotes.text: Three major tight oil plays in the Permian Basin—the Spraberry, Bone Spring, and Wolfcamp—accounted for 41% of U.S. tight oil production in 2018. In the AEO2019 Reference case, approximately half of cumulative tight oil production through 2050 is expected to come from these three plays. The Bakken and Eagle Ford plays also remain major contributors to U.S. tight oil supply through 2050, accounting for 19% and 17% of cumulative tight oil production, respectively.

reasons: AEO2019 shares directly answer the question; the combined comparison is arithmetic. These cumulative projected shares are distinct from the observed 2018 share.

question: How did the timing of the U.S. oil rig-count decline relative to falling crude oil prices in March 2020 differ from the historical response lag?

answer_points.text: Historically, oil rig counts followed oil-price changes with about a four-month lag. In March 2020, rigs began falling sharply by mid-March, during the same month as the price collapse, so the response was much faster.
WTI fell from $46.78/b at the start of March to $20.51/b at month-end, mostly in the first half; EIA linked the rapid rig response to sudden petroleum-demand losses from coronavirus mitigation.

quotes.text: Changes in the number of oil rigs have historically followed changes in oil prices with a lag time of about four months. However, the current drop in rig count followed the recent decrease in the oil price much more rapidly than in the past.

The spot price of West Texas Intermediate began March 2020 at $46.78 per barrel (b) and ended the month at $20.51/b; most of the decrease occurred in the first half of the month. The rig count began to decrease sharply in mid-March.
The quick reduction in active rigs reflects the sudden loss of petroleum demand related to coronavirus-related mitigation efforts

reasons: The cutoff-day account directly contrasts historical and observed rig timing. The six-month production-response lag in other passages describes a different outcome.

question: How did China's imports of light cycle oil and mixed aromatics, measured in barrels per day, change in July and August 2021 relative to their first-half averages following the June consumption-tax change?

answer_points.text: Light cycle oil imports fell from a first-half 2021 average of 390,000 b/d to 20,000 b/d in July and 30,000 b/d in August—declines of 370,000 and 360,000 b/d.
Mixed aromatics imports fell from a first-half average of 170,000 b/d to 70,000 b/d in July and 30,000 b/d in August—declines of 100,000 and 140,000 b/d.

quotes.text: Once the tax took effect, China’s imports of light cycle oil decreased from an average of 390,000 barrels per day (b/d) in the first six months of 2021 to 20,000 b/d in July and 30,000 b/d in August, the first two full months after the change in policy.
Similarly, China’s imports of mixed aromatics fell from an average of 170,000 b/d in the first six months of 2021 to 70,000 b/d in July and 30,000 b/d in August.

reasons: Eligible evidence gives both first-half baselines and July/August observations in barrels per day; absolute declines are direct subtraction.

question: How did U.S. distillate fuel oil exports to Europe change between the first halves of 2022 and 2023, and how did that compare with the change in total U.S. distillate exports and shipments to Central and South America?

answer_points.text: U.S. distillate exports to Europe increased from 56,000 b/d in the first half of 2022 to 138,000 b/d in the first half of 2023, an increase of 82,000 b/d, or approximately 146%.
Total U.S. distillate exports instead fell 5%, or 51,000 b/d, to 1.1 million b/d, led by lower shipments to Central and South America.

Central and South America remained the largest combined destination with 57% of U.S. distillate exports; increased European shipments partly reflected trade rerouting following sanctions on Russian petroleum products.

quotes.text: U.S. distillate fuel oil exports to destinations in Europe averaged 138,000 b/d in the first half of 2023 compared with 56,000 b/d in the first half of 2022.
The United States exported 1.1 million b/d of distillate fuel oil in 1H23, a 5% (51,000 b/d) decrease from the same time last year, led by lower exports to destinations in Central and South America
Despite the decrease, Central and South America combined remains the largest destination for U.S. distillate, accounting for 57% of all U.S. distillate exports.
The increase in distillate exports to Europe even as exports to other destinations declined partially reflects rerouted trade flows in response to sanctions on petroleum product imports from Russia.

reasons: The 2023 comparative accounts directly support the opposing regional and total trends. An older 2022 account reports 71,000 b/d for Europe; the answer uses the explicit 2023 comparisons, which both report 56,000 b/d.

question: How rapidly did Guyana's crude oil production grow on an annual-average basis during 2020–2023, and what production level and block concentration had it reached by early 2024?

answer_points.text: Guyana's crude oil production increased by an annual average of 98,000 b/d during 2020–2023, the third-fastest growth among non-OPEC producers.
By early 2024, crude oil production reached 645,000 b/d, entirely from the Stabroek block.

quotes.text: Guyana increased crude oil production by an annual average of 98,000 b/d from 2020 to 2023, making it the third-fastest growing non-OPEC producing country during this period.
Since starting production in 2019, Guyana has increased its crude oil production to 645,000 barrels per day (b/d) as of early 2024, all from the Stabroek block.

reasons: The cutoff-eligible May 2024 body directly supplies the historical growth rate, production level, and block concentration.

question: As of March 19, 2025, what production milestone had ConocoPhillips achieved at Alaska's Nuna project, and what statewide crude oil production increase and level did EIA forecast for 2026 with contributions expected from Nuna and Pikka?

answer_points.text: ConocoPhillips produced first oil from Nuna in December 2024.

EIA's March 2025 forecast projected Alaska crude oil production increasing by 16,000 b/d in 2026 to 438,000 b/d, with contributions expected from Nuna and Pikka; this was a forecast, not realized 2026 output.

quotes.text: ConocoPhillips produced first oil from the Nuna project in December 2024.

In our March 2025 Short-Term Energy Outlook , we forecast crude oil production in Alaska will increase by 16,000 barrels per day (b/d) in 2026 to 438,000 b/d after remaining relatively flat in 2025. Two new oil developments in Alaska—the Nuna and Pikka projects—are expected to boost crude oil production in the state after decades of decline.

reasons: The eligible evidence distinguishes Nuna's achieved first oil from the forecast statewide increase; later forecast revisions are excluded.

question: As of May 30, 2018, what crude oil reduction and production ceiling had OPEC agreed to under its November 2016 supply agreement, relative to which baseline, and how had the agreement's duration been extended?

answer_points.text: Under the November 2016 agreement, effective January 2017, OPEC agreed to reduce crude oil production by 1.2 million b/d relative to October 2016 and limit total production to 32.5 million b/d.
On November 30, 2017, OPEC and non-OPEC participants agreed to extend the cuts through the end of 2018.

quotes.text: As a result of the November 2016 OPEC supply agreement, which took effect in January 2017, OPEC member countries agreed to reduce crude oil production by 1.2 million barrels per day (b/d) compared with October 2016 levels and to limit total OPEC production to 32.5 million b/d.
OPEC and non-OPEC participants agreed on November 30, 2017, to extend the production cuts through the end of 2018 in an effort to reduce global oil inventories.

reasons: Eligible passages explicitly establish the reduction, baseline, ceiling, effective date, and extension; July 2018 changes are beyond the cutoff.

question: In EIA's April 2019 assessment, how did crude tanker size constrain use of the expanded Panama Canal for U.S. crude exports, and which alternative routes were expected to serve Asian and European destinations?

answer_points.text: The most commonly used crude tankers were too large for the expanded Panama Canal, which EIA expected to limit U.S. crude exports to the western coast of Central and South America.
EIA expected greater U.S. crude export volumes to reach Asia through the Suez Canal or around Africa's southern tip, and Europe by trans-Atlantic routes.

quotes.text: The most commonly used vessels to transport crude oil are too large to use the expanded Panama Canal. This restriction will likely limit flows of U.S. crude oil to destinations on the western coast of Central and South America.

Instead, greater volumes of U.S. crude oil exports are more likely to go to destinations in Asia through the Suez Canal or around the southern tip of Africa and to destinations in Europe using trans-Atlantic routes.

reasons: April 2019 evidence directly describes the size constraint and expected alternative routing; anticipated flows are not treated as observed shipments.

question: How much did Texas's proved reserves of crude oil and lease condensate increase on a net basis in 2018, and which Permian shale plays contributed the largest share of the increase?

answer_points.text: Texas's proved reserves of crude oil and lease condensate increased by a net 2.3 billion barrels in 2018, the largest state increase.
The Wolfcamp and Bone Spring shale plays in the Permian Basin contributed the largest share of the increase.

quotes.text: Texas saw the largest net increase in oil and natural gas proved reserves of all states in 2018, totaling 2.3 billion barrels of crude oil and lease condensate proved reserves and 22.9 Tcf of natural gas proved reserves.
The largest share of the increase was produced in the Wolfcamp and Bone Spring shale plays in the Permian Basin.

reasons: The eligible body gives the net reserves addition and named plays; barrels of reserves are distinct from production flows.

question: How did New Mexico operators' well shut-in and completion activity evolve between the first and second halves of 2020, and how did March 2021 crude oil production compare with the state's previous monthly record?

answer_points.text: In the first half of 2020, New Mexico operators shut in wells and limited new wells coming online amid the declining market; in the second half they resumed new well completion despite low prices.
March 2021 crude oil production averaged a record 1.16 million b/d, exceeding the previous monthly record set in November 2020.
